module.name: Individual Utility
module.description: This module represents the individual utility function. It implements Meta-Axioms 0.011–0.013 (Multi-dimensionality, Temporality, Context-dependence) as well as 0.041–0.042 (Time horizons and Uncertainty modulation) and 0.131 (Segment-specific weighting) from Module 7232. The individual utility function is defined as the first derivative of the meta-level. It integrates all relevant dimensions (FEPSDE) as well as mechanisms such as stress, social comparisons, technological disruptions, and ecological utility effects. This module forms the foundation of all individual analyses in BCM 2.0 and provides input for Awareness and Willingness processes. In every application, the WEIRD bias (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) must be explicitly considered to avoid misinterpretations due to cultural and institutional distortions. Status: production. Copyright: FehrAdvice & Partners AG, 2025.

A1.title: Module Context
A1.text: Chapter title: BCM2_01_INU – Individual Utility (v3.0, compliant with Meta-Axioms). This module represents the individual utility function and implements Meta-Axioms from Module 7232 including multi-dimensionality, temporality, context-dependence, time horizons, uncertainty modulation, and segment-specific weighting. It forms the foundation of all individual analyses in BCM 2.0 and provides input for Awareness and Willingness processes. The WEIRD bias must be explicitly considered in every application.

A2.title: Scope and Application
A2.text: This module applies to all individual utility functions in BCM simulations. Applicable in WEIRD contexts (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) and Non-WEIRD contexts (differing cultural, economic, and political frameworks). Represents individual evaluations in FEPSDE dimensions (financial, emotional, physical, social, digital, ecological). Encompasses analyses along four time horizons (instant, short-term, medium-term, long-term). Segment-specifically operationalizable (age, gender, socioeconomic status, life phases, culture). Supports intersectional segmentations. Foundation for scenarios with stress, coping, social comparisons, disruptions, and ecological utility effects. Serves as input for Awareness (7240) and Willingness functions (7243).

A3.title: Objectives and Function
A3.text: Objectives: Representation of individual pain and gain structures in FEPSDE dimensions according to Meta-Axiom 0.011. Integration of temporal horizons and discounting according to Meta-Axioms 0.012 and 0.041–0.042. Consideration of segment-specific differences according to Meta-Axiom 0.131. Representation of context-dependent effects according to Meta-Axiom 0.013. Integration of memory, learning, and dynamic adaptation. Consideration of cognitive biases, motivated beliefs, and blind spots. Embedding of stress and coping mechanisms as well as resilience functions. Representation of social comparison dynamics. Representation of technological disruption effects. Extension with ecological dimensions and sustainability factors. Provision of interface to Awareness (7240) and Willingness function (7243) for behavioral implementation.

A4.title: Binding Logic Rules - Individual Utility Axioms
A4.text: This section contains the formal axioms that define the binding logic rules for the Individual Utility module. These axioms establish foundational principles for individual utility modeling, including the master function, FEPSDE structure, loss aversion, baseline and intrinsic values, complementarities, reference points, time evaluation, uncertainty and risk, psychological mechanisms, dynamic adaptation, memory, willingness interface, salience, life phase and gender differentiation, cultural and institutional contexts, digital utility axis, habit dampening, intersectionality, stress and emotional regulation, social comparison dynamics, technological disruption, collateral effects, reaction time simulation, preference reconstruction, emotional valence, systemic feedback loops, bounded attention, self-control conflicts, spillover effects, physiological basic needs, bias corrections, moral preferences, identity investment, self-uncertainty, digital amplification, path dependence, meta-cognition, physical complementarity, social media addiction, and all dimensional complementarities within FEPSDE.

axioms.title: Master Function of Individual Value Function
axioms.formula: V_individual(a,t,k,s) = V_base(i) + Σ_{d∈FEPSDE} ω_d(t,s,k)[G_d(a,t) - λ_d(k,s) * P_d(a,t)] + C_intr,extr,idn(a,t,k,s) + CB(a,t,k,s) - CD(a,t,k,s) + RT_adj(a,t,k,s)
axioms.description: The individual value function of an action, activity, decision, behavior, or judgment results from integration of multiple levels: baseline value of activity, multidimensional gains and pains in FEPSDE, reference points and loss aversion, time dimension, segment and context dependence, dynamics through feedback and learning, collateral effects, and reaction time as measure of preference clarity. This represents the universal evaluation function that can be simulated for any individual action within BEATRIX.

axioms.title: FEPSDE Structure
axioms.formula: N_ind(t) = Σ_{d∈{fin, emo, phy, soc, dig, eco}} ω_d(t) [G_d(t) - λ_d * P_d(t)]
axioms.description: Individual value results from six dimensions: financial, emotional, physiological, social, digital, ecological. Each dimension has a weight, gains and losses are represented separately, modified by loss aversion and context factors. This axiom applies to all individual value functions and represents the multi-dimensionality of individual value, universally applicable in WEIRD and Non-WEIRD contexts.

axioms.title: Loss Aversion (Gain-Pain)
axioms.description: Losses are normally weighted more heavily than gains. The parameter λ can be greater than 1 (classical loss aversion), but also less than 1 (e.g., in masochism, asceticism, or athletic activities). This axiom applies to all dimensions of the FEPSDE structure and operationalizes the difference in weighting between gains and losses.

axioms.title: Baseline Value of Activity
axioms.description: Every activity has a basic value that does not need to be explained by rewards or specific activities. It encompasses psychological, social, emotional, and physiological basic needs that are fulfilled through activity. This axiom defines the basic value of human activity independent of specific tasks and forms the basis for distinguishing between intrinsic and extrinsic value.

axioms.title: Intrinsic Value of Specific Activity
axioms.description: The intrinsic value of an activity results from experiencing the activity itself. Activities can be positively intrinsic (joy, flow, meaning) or negative (boredom, overwhelm). This axiom models the utility that arises from the activity itself, particularly strong in psychological, social, emotional, and ecological dimensions, independent of extrinsic rewards.

axioms.title: Intrinsic Power Value
axioms.description: Individuals can derive utility from the mere exercise of power, even without instrumental benefits. This intrinsic power value reflects the psychological-emotional satisfaction from influence and control. This sub-axiom specifies the intrinsic value of specific activities and applies to contexts where exercising power itself is a source of psychological utility.

axioms.title: Extrinsic Value of Specific Activity
axioms.description: Extrinsic value results from rewards or external factors (e.g., money, recognition, status, security). It can strengthen intrinsic motivation (complementarity) or weaken it (crowding-out). This axiom captures all external rewards tied to an activity, particularly relevant for financial and reputation-based dimensions.

axioms.title: Complementarity of Value Functions
axioms.formula: V_total = V_base + V_intrinsic + V_extrinsic + κ(V_base, V_intrinsic, V_extrinsic)
axioms.description: The total value of an activity results not only from the addition of baseline, intrinsic, and extrinsic value, but also from their interactions. These can be complementary (mutual reinforcement) or substitutive (mutual weakening). This axiom applies universally to all activities and allows modeling of crowding-in and crowding-out effects.

axioms.title: Reference Points
axioms.description: Utility and disutility always arise relative to a reference point. This can be individual (e.g., income expectation), social (comparison with peers), or life-phase-dependent. If the reference point shifts, so does the evaluation. This axiom operationalizes the relative evaluation of utility and disutility, considering individual, social, and life-phase-dependent reference points.

axioms.title: Time Evaluation
axioms.formula: U_d(t) = Σ_{τ∈{inst, short, medium, long}} β_τ δ_τ^t U_{d,τ}(t)
axioms.description: Utility is weighted differently depending on time horizon. Short-term gains and losses are often disproportionately salient, while medium- and long-term effects are more heavily discounted. This enables modeling of impatience, procrastination, and foresight. This axiom models temporal evaluation and integrates different time horizons with both classical and hyperbolic discounting.

axioms.title: Uncertainty & Risk
axioms.description: Individual evaluations are always associated with uncertainty. Risk (known probabilities), ambiguity (unknown probabilities), and uncertainty (incomplete knowledge) reduce perceived value. The effect varies in strength across dimensions. This axiom describes value reduction through risk, ambiguity, and uncertainty, applying universally to all FEPSDE dimensions.

axioms.title: Motivated Beliefs
axioms.formula: B^M_d(t) = B^R_d(t) * (1 - γ_d * max(0, P_d(t) - T_d))
axioms.description: Individuals distort their beliefs when the truth would be too painful. This self-deception reduces short-term pain but can create long-term value losses. Motivated beliefs are a psychological protection mechanism. This axiom describes belief distortion to avoid disutility, particularly relevant for cognitive dissonance.

axioms.title: Blind Spots
axioms.description: Individuals do not consider all available information but selectively filter out aspects. These blind spots reduce the perceived value of an action or increase it when critical information is ignored. This axiom describes the effect of filtered-out information on individual value, allowing modeling of cognitive biases through information selection.

axioms.title: Dynamic Adaptation
axioms.description: Individual value continuously adapts to external feedback and context influences. This dynamic is central to explaining learning processes and habituation effects. This axiom models the ongoing adaptation of individual value functions, applying universally and allowing simulation of learning processes.

axioms.title: Memory
axioms.description: Previous experiences affect current evaluation. The influence decreases exponentially over time but persists. This explains the persistence of habits and trauma. This axiom models the aftereffect of previous experiences on current value, applying universally in all dimensions and varying by segment and context.

axioms.title: Willingness Interface
axioms.description: Individual value is input for the decision whether an action is actually performed. This occurs through a threshold function that represents sensitivity to context factors. This axiom connects individual value with action readiness and operationalizes the transition from value to behavior.

axioms.title: Salience
axioms.description: Immediate gains or losses are always salient, while medium- and long-term effects are only salient when activated by awareness. This axiom explains the tendency toward short-term thinking and describes the perceptibility of different time horizons.

axioms.title: Life Phase Dependence
axioms.description: The individual value of activities and decisions strongly depends on life phase. Needs, preferences, and sensitivities change along the life course. What has high value in youth may be irrelevant or negative in old age. This axiom considers biological, psychological, and social changes across the lifespan.

axioms.title: Gender Differentiation
axioms.description: Men, women, and non-binary persons have on average different utility structures. These differences can be biologically, socially, or culturally shaped. Gender differentiation allows more precise simulation of behavioral patterns and allows intersectional extensions.

axioms.title: Cultural & Institutional Contexts
axioms.description: Culture and institutions shape the perception of utility and disutility. What is valuable in one context can be worthless or even negative in another. This axiom operationalizes the dependence of individual value on cultural and institutional framework conditions.

axioms.title: Digital Utility Axis
axioms.description: Digitalization has created an independent utility axis. Individual value can be strongly influenced by digital aspects such as privacy, connectivity, reputation, and digital identity. This axiom defines digitality as an independent utility axis and supplements classical dimensions.

axioms.title: Habit Dampening
axioms.description: The more strongly an action is habitualized, the weaker new gains or pains have effect. Habits dampen the effect of changes and make behavior more inert. This axiom explains path dependencies and the difficulty of changing routines.

axioms.title: Intersectionality
axioms.formula: U_d(t) = f(Gender, Age, SES, Ethnicity, Culture, Institutions)
axioms.description: Individual value often results not from one affiliation alone but from the overlap of multiple dimensions such as gender, age, socioeconomic status, culture, or ethnicity. Intersectionality explains why some groups show particular vulnerability or resilience.

axioms.title: Stress & Emotional Regulation
axioms.description: Stress reduces individual value. Emotional regulation, coping strategies, and resilience act as buffers. This axiom explains why the same situation means hardly any value loss for some people while others suffer greatly.

axioms.title: Social Comparison Dynamics
axioms.description: People evaluate their value not absolutely but relative to peers. Comparison with others can increase utility (status gains) or create pain (status losses). Social comparison dynamics explain why inequality can have negative effects even with objective prosperity.

axioms.title: Technological Disruption
axioms.formula: U_d(t+1) = U_d(t) + Δ_disruption(t), Δ_disruption(t) = Shock(t) * σ_d
axioms.description: Technological shocks change value structures abruptly. They can create short-term pain (e.g., job loss) but also large long-term gains (e.g., productivity, health). This axiom explains the non-linear effect of innovation.

axioms.title: Collateral Damage
axioms.description: Every action can create unintended negative side effects. Collateral Damage describes these harmful effects that often occur in different dimensions than the intended gains. This axiom allows systematic integration of second-order effects.

axioms.title: Collateral Beauty
axioms.description: Every action can create unintended positive side effects. Collateral Beauty describes these positive effects that become visible in different dimensions than the original intention. This axiom complements Collateral Damage and allows balanced consideration.

axioms.title: Reaction Time Simulation (Time Will Tell Integration)
axioms.formula: RT_{i,j} = RT_i * RT_j * (1 / (1 + α * ΔV)) + ε
axioms.description: The reaction time of a decision is an endogenous function of preference clarity (ΔV), individual base speed, item difficulty, and stochastic noise factors. The stronger the difference in perceived value between two options, the faster the decision; the smaller the difference, the longer the decision takes.

axioms.title: Preference Reconstruction Under Noise
axioms.description: Individual preferences are latent and not directly observable. Decisions contain noise, which is why single choices are not sufficient to reconstruct stable preferences. By combining choice frequencies and process data such as reaction times, preferences can be estimated more reliably.

axioms.title: Item-Corrected Relative Reaction Time
axioms.description: The reaction time of a decision is only informative for preference strength when corrected for individual baseline speed and item-specific difficulty. This distinguishes between cognitive processing load and decision certainty.

axioms.title: Emotional Valence (Pride, Shame, Guilt)
axioms.formula: U_emotion(a,t) = ε_pride * Pride - ε_shame * Shame - ε_guilt * Guilt
axioms.description: Emotions like pride, shame, or guilt modulate the perception of gains and pains beyond the hot-vs-cold state. They act as amplifiers or dampeners on the individual value function.

axioms.title: Systemic Feedback Loops
axioms.description: Individual behavior changes context in the long term, whereby the individual value function is endogenously influenced. Behavior is thus not only an outcome but also input for future framework conditions.

axioms.title: Bounded Attention
axioms.description: Individuals can only process a subset of relevant information simultaneously. This limits the effective weighting of individual dimensions in the value function.

axioms.title: Self-Control Conflicts
axioms.description: Individuals have time inconsistencies between the long-term planning self (long-run self) and the short-term acting self (short-run self).

axioms.title: Spillover Effects
axioms.description: A behavior or decision in one domain positively or negatively affects utility in other domains. Spillover effects are central to multi-dimensional decisions.

axioms.title: Physiological Basic Needs as Foundation
axioms.formula: U_total(t) = f(BasePhysNeeds(t)) * Σ_d U_d(t), with f(BasePhysNeeds) ∈ [0,1]
axioms.description: The individual value function is hierarchically structured. Without a minimum level of physiological satisfaction (e.g., food, water, sleep, physical safety), higher utility components lose relevance or cannot be activated at all. This foundation acts as a constraint for all other utility components.

axioms.title: Bias Corrections (Cognitive Biases)
axioms.description: Individuals systematically deviate from rational evaluations because they are subject to cognitive biases (e.g., status quo bias, framing effects, overconfidence, anchoring). These biases change the weighting of gain and pain and act like transformations on the value function.

axioms.title: Moral Preferences (Altruism, Revenge, Reciprocity)
axioms.formula: U_moral(t) = ε_altruism * U_other_gain - ε_spite * U_other_gain + ε_recip * f(Fairness_dev)
axioms.description: Besides individual, collective, and identity utility, values arise from moral preferences. Individuals experience positive utility when helping others (altruism) or restoring fairness (reciprocity), and can also derive utility from punishing unfair behavior (revenge).

axioms.title: Intertemporal Identity Investment
axioms.formula: U_ID(t) = β_ID * Σ_{τ>t} δ^{τ-t} * Consistency(Self_future(τ), Action(t))
axioms.description: Individuals evaluate actions not only by immediate gain but also by how strongly they contribute to long-term identity formation. Decisions act as investments in the future self and create utility through congruence with a desired self-image.

axioms.title: Self-Uncertainty (Noisy Preferences)
axioms.description: Individual preferences are not stable fixed points but are influenced by uncertainty, cognitive limitations, and stochastic processes. Decisions can therefore appear inconsistent even when based on the same preference system.

axioms.title: Digital Amplification (Social Media Reinforcement)
axioms.description: Digital systems amplify emotions, preferences, and identity markers through algorithmic selection and feedback loops. Likes, shares, and algorithmically personalized content cause small differences in preferences or emotions to be disproportionately amplified.

axioms.title: Path Dependence & Irreversibility
axioms.formula: U_total(t+1) = U_total(t) + φ_path * PastChoices(t) - φ_irrev * LostOptions(t)
axioms.description: Individual decisions are not isolated but have long-term feedback effects on one's own utility function. Path dependencies arise when a once-chosen option systematically influences the probability of future options. Irreversibility occurs when certain decisions permanently change the value function.

axioms.title: Meta-Cognition (Self-Evaluation)
axioms.formula: U_meta(t) = η_pos * Consistency(Self(t), Action(t)) - η_neg * Inconsistency(Self(t), Action(t))
axioms.description: Individuals observe their own actions and reconstruct a self-image from them. Depending on whether action and self-image are consistent or inconsistent, additional utility (pride, self-affirmation) or disutility (shame, guilt, dissonance) arises.

axioms.title: Physical Complementarity
axioms.formula: U_d_eff(t) = U_d(t) * φ_phys(Health(t)), d ∈ {fin, emo, phy, soc, dig, eco}
axioms.description: The physical dimension (health, energy, pain, vitality) acts as a multiplicative base effect on all other utility axes. Deficits reduce, surplus amplifies the effective utility of other dimensions.

axioms.title: Social Media Addiction (Digital Addiction)
axioms.formula: U_digital(t+1) = U_digital(t) + α_add * Reward(t) - β_cost * Spillover(t)
axioms.description: Social media and digital platforms are designed to activate addiction mechanisms. Repeated usage reinforces short-term emotional and social utility but can simultaneously create long-term ecological, social, and psychological disutility.

axioms.title: Financial ↔ Emotional Complementarity
axioms.description: Financial utility unfolds more strongly when it also creates emotional security or joy (e.g., gift vs. money). Conversely, emotional stress amplifies the negative effects of financial losses.

axioms.title: Financial ↔ Psychological Complementarity
axioms.description: Financial reward works more strongly when it strengthens psychological self-efficacy. Financial losses weigh more heavily when psychologically associated with failure.

axioms.title: Financial ↔ Social Complementarity
axioms.description: Money often has social value (status, recognition, participation). A financial gain amplifies social utility, a loss weakens it.

axioms.title: Financial ↔ Digital Complementarity
axioms.description: Digital goods and infrastructures gain value when financially accessible. Financial gains can enable digital self-actualization.

axioms.title: Financial ↔ Ecological Complementarity
axioms.description: Sustainable investments have high value when financially viable. Financial gains increase the scope for ecologically motivated decisions.

axioms.title: Emotional ↔ Psychological Complementarity
axioms.description: Emotional states are closely linked to psychological self-perception. Joy strengthens self-efficacy, stress weakens it.

axioms.title: Emotional ↔ Social Complementarity
axioms.description: Emotional experiences are often socially shaped. Joy or shame unfold more strongly in social contexts.

axioms.title: Emotional ↔ Digital Complementarity
axioms.description: Digital interactions can trigger strong emotional reactions (likes, shitstorms). Emotions amplify the value of digital experiences.

axioms.title: Emotional ↔ Ecological Complementarity
axioms.description: Emotional bonds (e.g., climate shame or pride in sustainable action) amplify the effect of ecological decisions.

axioms.title: Psychological ↔ Social Complementarity
axioms.description: Psychological self-efficacy is reinforced through social recognition. Lack of social feedback can diminish psychological utility.

axioms.title: Psychological ↔ Digital Complementarity
axioms.description: Digital competencies unfold value when psychologically perceived as self-efficacy.

axioms.title: Psychological ↔ Ecological Complementarity
axioms.description: Sustainable behavior can create psychological meaningfulness. Lack of ecological responsibility can amplify psychological dissonance.

axioms.title: Social ↔ Digital Complementarity
axioms.description: Digital platforms unfold value primarily through social interactions (e.g., social media).

axioms.title: Social ↔ Ecological Complementarity
axioms.description: Social recognition amplifies ecologically motivated decisions. Ecological responsibility unfolds social status value.

axioms.title: Digital ↔ Ecological Complementarity
axioms.description: Digital technologies can amplify ecological utility (e.g., through efficiency gains) or weaken it (e.g., energy consumption).

A5.title: Prerequisites and Requirements
A5.text: Pain and gain data in all FEPSDE dimensions according to Meta-Axiom 0.011. Explicit reference points for each dimension (individual, social, life-phase-dependent) according to Meta-Axiom 0.013. Discounting parameters and time proxies (instant, short-term, medium-term, long-term) according to Meta-Axioms 0.012 and 0.041–0.042. Uncertainty and risk parameters according to Meta-Axiom 0.042. Segment parameters: age, gender, socioeconomic status, life phase, culture, institutions according to Meta-Axiom 0.131. Intersectional identity positions. Coping and resilience values for modeling stress effects. Data on social comparison groups (peers, reference groups). Trigger parameters for technological disruptions. Ecological utility values (sustainability, resource usage, environmental impact). Digital utility components (privacy, connectivity, reputation, identity).

A6.title: Structure Integration and Linkages
A6.text: Meta modules: 7232 META, 9232 STD. Awareness and Willingness: 7240 AWX, 7243 WAX. Utility modules: 7235 KNU (Collective Utility), 7236 IDN (Identity Utility). Context and Segment: 8904 KON, 7257 SEG. Life Journeys: 7457 LCP, 7256 JNY. Uncertainty and Complexity: 9485 UNS_META, 9486 UNS_ENV, 9495 UNS_IPN, 9493 UNS_INS, 9494 UNS_EPI, 9492 KOM_META. Intervention and Monitoring: 9250 INT, 9251 WATCHDOG. Extended Logics: 9477 STA, 9479 SPT, 9480 GAM.

A7.title: Semantic Boundaries and Limitations
A7.text: This module exclusively represents individual utility. Collective utility (7235) and identity utility (7236) are separate modules and are not considered here. External framework conditions (e.g., institutional structures, regulatory requirements) are only integrated insofar as they affect individual utility perceptions (Reference: 8904 KON, 9493 UNS_INS). The aggregation of individual utility functions to group or societal utility occurs exclusively via 7235 (KNU). The anchoring of individual utility functions in identities or affiliations occurs exclusively via 7236 (IDN). This module is not responsible for deriving or operationalizing interventions – it provides input values for 9250 (INT).

A8.title: Versioning and Validity
A8.text: Version history: v1.0 – Original version 7234: Introduction of individual utility function along FEPS dimensions with Pain/Gain separation. v1.1 – Structural conformity according to 9232 (A1–A10 introduced). v2.0 – Extension with gender, life phase, and culture dependencies; introduction of digital dimension. v2.1 – Integration of intersectionality (combination of gender, age, SES, culture, institutions). v2.2 – Extension with stress, coping, and resilience mechanisms. v2.3 – Integration of social comparison dynamics. v2.4 – Modeling of technological disruptions as utility shocks. v2.5 – Introduction of ecological dimension (FEPSDE logic, sustainability). v3.0 – Complete linkage to 7232 (Meta-Axioms: Multi-dimensionality, Temporality, Context, Time horizons, Segment logic), explicit consideration of WEIRD bias and clarification of module connections.
